title: Management Cybernetics is the new Public Choice Theory
abstract: From Designing Freedom, and Stafford’s ideas on governance on a democratic society suggest how, starting from the existing theory of public choice, Beer’s cybernetic perspective can help us design better and more productive public institutions.

title: Organizing for Autonomy: The Viable System Model as a Framework for Becoming an AI-Native Company
abstract: Purpose: Most corporate AI programs fail for organizational reasons. MIT (2025) reports that 95 percent of generative AI pilots show no measurable profit effect. Deloitte (2026) finds that 85 percent of firms plan to adapt AI agents while 21 percent have a governance model for them. This contribution asks why and how the Viable System Model can guide companies that want to become AI-native. Methods: The study uses reverse engineering. It builds a requirements list from Martin Hofmann’s book The Agentic Enterprise (2026) and nine industry reports from McKinsey, BCG, Deloitte, Anthropic, and OpenAI, covering more than 20,000 executive respondents. It maps the list onto the five VSM systems and applies Perez Rios’ Taxonomy of Organizational Pathologies to the documented failure patterns. Findings: The requirements match the five systems closely. Coordination layers for agents correspond to System 2, governance at machine speed to Systems 3 and 3*, and leadership models to System 5. The consulting firms describe these functions without naming Beer. Three gaps appear: a missing System 4 function, no formal rule for recursion, and undesigned variety flows at human-agent interfaces. Fourteen pathologies connect the failure patterns to structural causes and named interventions. Implications: The VSM gives companies a diagnosis of AI failure and construction rules for organizations in which autonomous agents can work at scale. The contribution proposes six design principles and a research agenda, including the question of which System 5 decisions must stay human.

title: Cybernetics of Community Development – A TEAM (Thinking with Every Available Mind) Activity
abstract: My contributions to establishing the Bloomfield Community Centre in Narberth, Pembrokeshire (1980s), and founding the Todmorden Learning Centre in West Yorkshire (2010s) have led to the understanding presented here.  The two central themes of community development:- providing opportunities for establishing and developing relationships between members of the community; understanding successful democratic cooperative managing of the processes involved; viz- Creating a community hub where members of the community can meet so that new relationships are made and old relationships are strengthened. The hub must be welcoming to all, drawing people in to enjoy themselves, discuss problems, and begin the tasks of improving the community. The hub should become a seeding ground for ideas, and collective help, establishing community enterprises which are grounded in supporting the community and in cooperative ideals. This will lessen dependence on outside provision of the necessary goods and services that are required by the community. Ensuring the ideals and culture developed in the hub become those of the formal community government will further enable development towards sustainability, opening the possibility of new funding. Spreading the ideas and culture of sustainability and cooperation to surrounding communities, helping build their communities toward sustainability will strengthen our community in trading locally, gathering new ideas, and helping others. Working together with neighbouring communities when they have achieved the first four stages of this journey will enable this culture and way of being to move to the next level of governing.

title: Beyond Viability: Ontological Foundations for Ethical and Regenerative Systems
abstract: Purpose: This paper argues that resilient, ethical, and regenerative systems cannot be fully understood without examining the assumptions on which they are built. By ontology, the paper refers to the underlying assumptions a system makes about human beings, value, relationship, responsibility, and the wider living world. Methods: The paper develops a conceptual and practice-oriented argument drawing on organisational cybernetics, systems thinking, institutional analysis, and practitioner reflection. It examines how different ontological assumptions shape system purpose, feedback, accountability, incentive design, and definitions of viability. Particular attention is given to the contrast between separative assumptions, where actors, organisations, and ecosystems are treated as largely independent units, and relational assumptions, where agency is understood within shared fields of consequence. Findings: The paper suggests that systems built on fragmented assumptions tend to reproduce fragmented responsibility, externalised harm, procedural compliance, and short-term adaptation without deeper regeneration. Under pressure, ethical commitments become fragile when added as policy layers rather than embedded in the system’s foundational logic. Implications/Contributions: The paper contributes to discussions on viable and regenerative systems by proposing ontology as a practical design layer. It argues that sustainable governance requires coherence between what a system claims to preserve and what its underlying assumptions actually make possible. Ethical viability therefore depends on more coherent assumptions about interdependence, responsibility, and shared life.

title: Midlife Chrysalis: from ‘good Chinese boy’ and economics to Stafford Beer-aholics
abstract: From expert economic witness testifying and citing The Nature of the Firm (Coase) to courts and antitrust regulators in high-stakes litigation; to discombobulated PhD student interpreting The Brain of the Firm (Beer) to diagnose ‘System 3*s’ in green building rating organisations. I reflect on my transition from ‘a good Chinese boy’ gainfully employed as a policy/regulatory economist advising on ‘optimal pathways’, to liquefying my DNA inside an untested transdisciplinary chrysalis, to the throes of turning cybernetic and learning to accept: ‘no hay camino, se hace camino al andar.’ [there is no road; you make your own path as you walk.] Somewhere along the way—between piloting the Master of Applied Cybernetics at the Australian National University (ANU), watching my country in flames, starting a cohort based PhD programme, locking down amidst a global pandemic and drafting a research agenda for a new School of Cybernetics (SOCY)—I stumbled into Stafford Beer. The Viable System Model (VSM) is now core to my research to develop new theory and praxis on viable sociotechnical/sustainability transition intermediary organisations for transforming our buildings and cities. As the School’s de facto Chief Beer Officer (CBO), I will also celebrate some new research from fellow travellers also inspired by Stafford Beer. SOCY PhD students who have adopted and adapted the Viable System Model (VSM) to generate novel insights for how to viably manage sociotechnical systems, such as ‘smart’ street lighting infrastructure, and decision making structures of early-stage venture capital firms in the age of AI.
